headline: Study Confirms Printers Only Function When Verbally Threatened
subheadline: Researchers document 847% improvement in print success rate after 'aggressive negotiation'
summary: A peer-reviewed study has validated what office workers have long suspected: printers respond to intimidation.
content:
A groundbreaking study from the Institute of Applied Technology has confirmed what office workers have known for decades: printers are significantly more likely to function when verbally threatened.

The study, titled "Coercive Communication and Peripheral Device Performance," monitored 500 office printers across 47 workplaces over six months. Researchers documented printer behavior under various conditions, including polite requests, neutral commands, and what they clinically termed "escalating verbal hostility."

The results were unambiguous.

"Printers that received polite requests completed print jobs 34% of the time," explained lead researcher Dr. Amanda Foster. "Printers that were threatened with physical violence completed jobs 89% of the time. When researchers mentioned 'replacement,' success rates jumped to 94%."

The study also found that printer performance improved when users maintained eye contact with the device, referred to it by name (even if the name was an expletive), and made credible references to "knowing someone in IT."

"We cannot explain why this works," Dr. Foster admitted. "Printers don't have ears. They don't have feelings. And yet." She gestured at a laser printer that had successfully printed her slides only after she called it "a waste of plastic that would look great in a dumpster."

The findings have prompted some workplaces to implement "designated printer negotiators"—employees skilled in the art of technological intimidation.

"I don't even work here anymore," said Marcus Chen, a former Omnicorp Holdings employee who still visits his old office twice a week. "They just bring me in when the HP acts up. I look at it. It prints. That's the arrangement."

At press time, 847 office workers had reported that their printers had "started behaving" immediately after reading this article aloud near the device.
author: Sandra Mitchell, Technology Reporter
